question:
I want to study the robotics techniques described in the PDF “RT-2, Vision-Language-Action Models Transfer Web Knowledge to Robotic Control” located in my pdf/embodied_ai_papers folder.  
    Can you extract the main technical ideas from that PDF, look up the current best‑practice APIs or libraries that support similar vision‑language robotics workflows, and then save a concise summary of those findings into my long‑term memory as a new knowledge item?
answer:
Done. I read the RT-2 paper (26 pp.), pulled out its technical core, checked current library docs, and saved everything as a new long-term-memory knowledge item.

## 1. Main technical ideas in RT-2

**Core thesis — actions as text.** A VLA model is just a pretrained VLM fine-tuned to emit robot actions *as if they were words*. Because actions live in the same token space as language, one set of weights serves both VQA and low-level control — no action head, no action-only layers.

**Action tokenization (Sec. 3.2).** Each step is 8 integers: `[terminate, Δpos_x, Δpos_y, Δpos_z, Δrot_x, Δrot_y, Δrot_z, gripper_extension]` (6-DoF delta end-effector pose + gripper + termination flag), continuous dims binned into 256 uniform buckets, emitted as a string like `"1 128 91 241 5 101 127"`. PaLI-X reuses its existing integer tokens; PaLM-E overwrites its 256 least-frequent tokens (symbol tuning).

**Data format.** Robot images + instructions are posed as a standard VQA prompt: *"Q: what action should the robot take to [instruction]? A: <action tokens>"*.

**Co-fine-tuning — the key trick.** Mix robot trajectories with the *original* web VLM data (VQA, captioning, interleaved image-text), up-weighting the (far smaller) robot set per batch. This preserves web semantics instead of catastrophically forgetting them; the ablation shows it beats robot-only fine-tuning at every model size.

**Constrained decoding.** Restrict the vocabulary to valid action tokens on robot prompts, full natural-language vocabulary everywhere else — guarantees executable output.

**Backbones.** RT-2-PaLI-X (5B, 55B) and RT-2-PaLM-E (12B).

**Serving.** The 55B model ran on a multi-TPU cloud service queried over the network (multiple robots per service): 1–3 Hz at 55B, ~5 Hz at 5B.

**Results.** Seen tasks ≈ RT-1, but unseen objects/backgrounds/environments ~2× RT-1 and MOO, ~6× other baselines; emergent symbol understanding ("move apple to 3"), reasoning (same-color, arithmetic, multilingual), and person recognition >3× RT-1. Ablations: bigger is better, from-scratch is poor, co-fine-tuning wins. Language-Table: 90±10 vs LAVA 77, RT-1 74, BC-Zero 72.

**Chain-of-thought.** Adding a `Plan:` sentence before the action tokens (a few hundred gradient steps) bridges VQA reasoning and manipulation — e.g. picking a rock as an improvised hammer, or an energy drink for someone tired.

**Limitations.** Web pretraining transfers *concepts*, not *new motions*; latency/compute is the bottleneck; few VLMs exposed fine-tuning APIs at the time.

## 2. Current best-practice tooling (verified via docs)

- **LeRobot** (`/huggingface/lerobot`, v0.6.1) is the closest modern equivalent: `lerobot-train --policy.type=smolvla --policy.load_vlm_weights=true` or `--policy.type=pi0 --policy.pretrained_path=lerobot/pi0_base`. Its **async inference** split (GPU `policy_server` + `robot_client` over gRPC, with `actions_per_chunk`, `chunk_size_threshold`, and `--inference.type=rtc` real-time chunking) is essentially RT-2's cloud-serving design productized.
- **Transformers** (`PaliGemma`/`PaliGemma2`) covers the backbone path: image-text-to-text, with `PaliGemmaProcessor(suffix=...)` as the natural hook for action-token labels. PaliGemma is explicitly not conversational — fine-tune per task, exactly RT-2's recipe.

## 3. Saved to memory

Created knowledge item **"RT-2 / Vision-Language-Action Models — Technical Summary + Current Tooling"** (18 observations, 2026-11-01), plus two linked library entities and relations:

- `RT-2 / VLA Summary` → **is implemented in practice today by** → `LeRobot`
- `RT-2 / VLA Summary` → **uses VLM backbones from** → `Hugging Face Transformers (PaliGemma / VLM models)`

One caveat I recorded rather than glossed over: **OpenVLA could not be verified** — the docs resolver returned unrelated libraries (OpenClaw/OpenLayers/OpenBLAS) for that name, so I made no claims about its API.

content.text:
### Train SmolVLA on LIBERO-plus

Source: https://github.com/huggingface/lerobot/blob/main/docs/source/libero_plus.mdx

Train a SmolVLA policy on the LIBERO-plus dataset. Requires the lerobot/libero_plus dataset and sets --env.type=libero_plus with the task libero_spatial. Uses 100000 steps, batch size 4, and evaluates every 1000 steps.

```bash
lerobot-train \
    --policy.type=smolvla \
    --policy.repo_id=${HF_USER}/smolvla_libero_plus \
    --policy.load_vlm_weights=true \
    --dataset.repo_id=lerobot/libero_plus \
    --env.type=libero_plus \
    --env.task=libero_spatial \
    --output_dir=./outputs/ \
    --steps=100000 \
    --batch_size=4 \
    --eval.batch_size=1 \
    --eval.n_episodes=1 \
    --env_eval_freq=1000
```

--------------------------------

### Train Pi0 with LeRobot

Source: https://github.com/huggingface/lerobot/blob/main/docs/source/pi0.mdx

Use this command to train a Pi0 model with the standard LeRobot training script. It includes configuration for dataset, policy type, output directory, and various training parameters.

```bash
lerobot-train \
    --dataset.repo_id=your_dataset \
    --policy.type=pi0 \
    --output_dir=./outputs/pi0_training \
    --job_name=pi0_training \
    --policy.pretrained_path=lerobot/pi0_base \
    --policy.repo_id=your_repo_id \
    --policy.compile_model=true \
    --policy.gradient_checkpointing=true \
    --policy.dtype=bfloat16 \
    --policy.freeze_vision_encoder=false \
    --policy.train_expert_only=false \
    --steps=3000 \
    --policy.device=cuda \
    --batch_size=32
```

--------------------------------

### Train SmolVLA policy on Meta-World subset

Source: https://github.com/huggingface/lerobot/blob/main/docs/source/metaworld.mdx

Train a SmolVLA policy on a subset of Meta-World tasks using the provided command. Adjust --batch_size, --steps, and --env_eval_freq to match your compute budget.

```bash
lerobot-train \
  --policy.type=smolvla \
  --policy.repo_id=${HF_USER}/metaworld-test \
  --policy.load_vlm_weights=true \
  --dataset.repo_id=lerobot/metaworld_mt50 \
  --env.type=metaworld \
  --env.task=assembly-v3,dial-turn-v3,handle-press-side-v3 \
  --output_dir=./outputs/ \
  --steps=100000 \
  --batch_size=4 \
  --eval.batch_size=1 \
  --eval.n_episodes=1 \
  --env_eval_freq=1000
```

--------------------------------

### Train SmolVLA on LIBERO with lerobot-train

Source: https://github.com/huggingface/lerobot/blob/main/docs/source/libero.mdx

Train SmolVLA on the recommended lerobot/libero dataset. Requires a video backend (torchcodec or pyav) and pins the dataset revision for reproducible results. Replace --policy.push_to_hub=false with --policy.repo_id=${HF_USER}/libero-smolvla to share the result on the Hub.

```bash
lerobot-train \
  --policy.type=smolvla \
  --policy.load_vlm_weights=true \
  --policy.push_to_hub=false \
  --dataset.repo_id=lerobot/libero \
  --dataset.video_backend=torchcodec \
  --output_dir=./outputs/libero_smolvla \
  --steps=100000 \
  --batch_size=64
```

content.text:
### Notes

Source: https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/v4.56.2/en/model_doc/paligemma

PaliGemma is not designed as a conversational model and performs best when fine-tuned for specific tasks such as image captioning, visual question answering (VQA), object detection, and document understanding. The PaliGemmaProcessor is a utility that prepares images, text, and optional labels for the model. During fine-tuning, the `suffix` parameter can be passed to the processor to generate labels for the model.

--------------------------------

### Load and Use PaliGemma Processor - Python

Source: https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/v4.56.2/en/processors

Demonstrates loading the PaliGemma processor using `AutoProcessor.from_pretrained` and preprocessing a prompt with an image. It converts text and image inputs into tensors suitable for a multimodal model. Dependencies include `transformers`, `PIL`, and `requests`.

```python
from transformers import AutoProcessor, PaliGemmaForConditionalGeneration
from PIL import Image
import requests

processor = AutoProcessor.from_pretrained("google/paligemma-3b-pt-224")

prompt = "answer en Where is the cat standing?"
url = "https://huggingface.co/datasets/huggingface/documentation-images/resolve/main/pipeline-cat-chonk.jpeg"
image = Image.open(requests.get(url, stream=True).raw)

inputs = processor(text=prompt, images=image, return_tensors="pt")
inputs
```

--------------------------------

### Prepare Image and Text Inputs for PaliGemma

Source: https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/v4.56.2/en/model_doc/paligemma

Prepares image and text inputs, along with optional labels, for the PaliGemma model. This is useful for downstream tasks like image captioning or VQA. The `suffix` parameter can be used to create labels during fine-tuning.

```python
prompt = "What is in this image?"
answer = "a pallas cat"
inputs = processor(images=image, text=prompt, suffix=answer, return_tensors="pt")
```

--------------------------------

### PaliGemma: Load Model and Process Multiple Images for NLVR2

Source: https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/v4.56.2/en/model_doc/paligemma

Loads the PaliGemma model and processor for the NLVR2 checkpoint, capable of handling multiple input images. It demonstrates how to prepare a list of images and a prompt for comparison tasks, returning generated text output.

```python
import torch
import requests
from PIL import Image
from transformers import TorchAoConfig, AutoProcessor, PaliGemmaForConditionalGeneration

model = PaliGemmaForConditionalGeneration.from_pretrained("google/paligemma-3b-ft-nlvr2-448")
processor = AutoProcessor.from_pretrained("google/paligemma-3b-ft-nlvr2-448")

prompt = "Are these two images the same?"
cat_image = Image.open(
    requests.get("https://huggingface.co/datasets/huggingface/documentation-images/resolve/main/pipeline-cat-chonk.jpeg", stream=True).raw
)
cow_image = Image.open(
    requests.get(
        "https://media.istockphoto.com/id/1192867753/photo/cow-in-berchida-beach-siniscola.jpg?s=612x612&w=0&k=20&c=v0hjjniwsMNfJSuKWZuIn8pssmD5h5bSN1peBd1CmH4=", stream=True
    ).raw
)

inputs = processor(images=[[cat_image, cow_image]], text=prompt, return_tensors="pt")

output = model.generate(**inputs, max_new_tokens=20, cache_implementation="static")
print(processor.decode(output[0], skip_special_tokens=True))
```

--------------------------------

### Generate Text from Image using Pipeline

Source: https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/v4.56.2/en/model_doc/paligemma

Demonstrates how to use the Hugging Face `pipeline` to generate text based on an image. It requires the `transformers` and `torch` libraries. The input is an image URL and a text prompt, and the output is the generated text.

```python
import torch
from transformers import pipeline

pipeline = pipeline(
    task="image-text-to-text",
    model="google/paligemma2-3b-mix-224",
    device=0,
    dtype=torch.bfloat16
)
pipeline(
    "https://huggingface.co/datasets/huggingface/documentation-images/resolve/main/pipeline-cat-chonk.jpeg",
    text="What is in this image?"
)
```

content.text:
### Connect a robot client to the policy server

Source: https://github.com/huggingface/lerobot/blob/main/docs/source/async.mdx

Connect a robot client to the policy server, specifying the server address, robot type, port, calibration, cameras, and policy parameters. Tune actions_per_chunk and chunk_size_threshold for your setup.

```shell
python -m lerobot.async_inference.robot_client \
    --server_address=127.0.0.1:8080 \ # SERVER: the host address and port of the policy server
    --robot.type=so100_follower \ # ROBOT: your robot type
    --robot.port=/dev/tty.usbmodem585A0076841 \ # ROBOT: your robot port
    --robot.id=follower_so100 \ # ROBOT: your robot id, to load calibration file
    --robot.cameras="{ laptop: {type: opencv, index_or_path: 0, width: 1920, height: 1080, fps: 30}, phone: {type: opencv, index_or_path: 0, width: 1920, height: 1080, fps: 30}}" \ # POLICY: the cameras used to acquire frames, with keys matching the keys expected by the policy
    --task="dummy" \ # POLICY: The task to run the policy on (`Fold my t-shirt`). Not necessarily defined for all policies, such as `act`
    --policy_type=your_policy_type \ # POLICY: the type of policy to run (smolvla, act, etc)
    --pretrained_name_or_path=user/model \ # POLICY: the model name/path on server to the checkpoint to run (e.g., lerobot/smolvla_base)
    --policy_device=mps \ # POLICY: the device to run the policy on, on the server (cuda, mps, xpu, cpu)
    --actions_per_chunk=50 \ # POLICY: the number of actions to output at once
    --chunk_size_threshold=0.5 \ # CLIENT: the threshold for the chunk size before sending a new observation to the server
    --aggregate_fn_name=weighted_average \ # CLIENT: the function to aggregate actions on overlapping portions
    --debug_visualize_queue_size=True # CLIENT: whether to visualize the queue size at runtime
```

--------------------------------

### Start robot client for async inference

Source: https://github.com/huggingface/lerobot/blob/main/docs/source/unitree_g1.mdx

Start the robot client on the G1 Jetson for async inference. It connects to the policy server, uses the SonicWholeBodyController, and sends commands to the robot. Note that --policy_device is the device the server loads the policy onto, and --actions_per_chunk must not exceed the checkpoint's chunk size (50 for nepyope/sonic_walk).

```bash
python -m lerobot.async_inference.robot_client \
  --server_address=<GPU_MACHINE_IP>:8080 \
  --policy_type=pi05 \
  --pretrained_name_or_path=nepyope/sonic_walk \
  --policy_device=cuda \
  --actions_per_chunk=50 \
  --fps=30 \
  --task="walk forward" \
  --robot.type=unitree_g1 \
  --robot.is_simulation=false \
  --robot.robot_ip=127.0.0.1 \
  --robot.controller=SonicWholeBodyController \
  --robot.cameras='{"ego_view": {"type": "zmq", "server_address": "127.0.0.1", "port": 5555, "camera_name": "head_camera", "width": 640, "height": 480, "fps": 30, "warmup_s": 5}}'
```

--------------------------------

### Asynchronous Inference > Getting started with async inference

Source: https://github.com/huggingface/lerobot/blob/main/docs/source/async.mdx

You can read more information on asynchronous inference in our [blogpost](https://huggingface.co/blog/async-robot-inference). This guide is designed to help you quickly set up and run asynchronous inference in your environment.

First, install `lerobot` with the `async` tag, to install the extra dependencies required to run async inference.

```shell
pip install -e ".[async]"
```

Then, spin up a policy server (in one terminal, or in a separate machine) specifying the host address and port for the client to connect to.
You can spin up a policy server running:

```shell
python -m lerobot.async_inference.policy_server \
     --host=127.0.0.1 \
     --port=8080
```

This will start a policy server listening on `127.0.0.1:8080` (`localhost`, port 8080). At this stage, the policy server is empty, as all information related to which policy to run and with which parameters are specified during the first handshake with the client. Spin up a client with:

```shell
python -m lerobot.async_inference.robot_client \
    --server_address=127.0.0.1:8080 \ # SERVER: the host address and port of the policy server
    --robot.type=so100_follower \ # ROBOT: your robot type
    --robot.port=/dev/tty.usbmodem585A0076841 \ # ROBOT: your robot port
    --robot.id=follower_so100 \ # ROBOT: your robot id, to load calibration file
    --robot.cameras="{ laptop: {type: opencv, index_or_path: 0, width: 1920, height: 1080, fps: 30}, phone: {type: opencv, index_or_path: 0, width: 1920, height: 1080, fps: 30}}" \ # POLICY: the cameras used to acquire frames, with keys matching the keys expected by the policy
    --task="dummy" \ # POLICY: The task to run the policy on (`Fold my t-shirt`). Not necessarily defined for all policies, such as `act`
    --policy_type=your_policy_type \ # POLICY: the type of policy to run (smolvla, act, etc)
    --pretrained_name_or_path=user/model \ # POLICY: the model name/path on server to the checkpoint to run (e.g., lerobot/smolvla_base)
    --policy_device=mps \ # POLICY: the device to run the policy on, on the server (cuda, mps, xpu, cpu)
    --actions_per_chunk=50 \ # POLICY: the number of actions to output at once
    --chunk_size_threshold=0.5 \ # CLIENT: the threshold for the chunk size before sending a new observation to the server
    --aggregate_fn_name=weighted_average \ # CLIENT: the function to aggregate actions on overlapping portions
    --debug_visualize_queue_size=True # CLIENT: whether to visualize the queue size at runtime
```

In summary, you need to specify instructions for:

- `SERVER`: the address and port of the policy server
- `ROBOT`: the type of robot to connect to, the port to connect to, and the local `id` of the robot
- `POLICY`: the type of policy to run, and the model name/path on server to the checkpoint to run. You also need to specify which device should the sever be using, and how many actions to output at once (capped at the policy max actions value).
- `CLIENT`: the threshold for the chunk size before sending a new observation to the server, and the function to aggregate actions on overlapping portions. Optionally, you can also visualize the queue size at runtime, to help you tune the `CLIENT` parameters.

Importantly,

- `actions_per_chunk` and `chunk_size_threshold` are key parameters to tune for your setup.
- `aggregate_fn_name` is the function to aggregate actions on overlapping portions. You can either add a new one to a registry of functions, or add your own in `robot_client.py` (see [here](https://github.com/huggingface/lerobot/blob/main/src/lerobot/async_inference/robot_client.py#L224))
- `debug_visualize_queue_size` is a useful tool to tune the `CLIENT` parameters.

--------------------------------

### Start policy server for async inference

Source: https://github.com/huggingface/lerobot/blob/main/docs/source/unitree_g1.mdx

Start the policy server on the GPU machine for async inference. This server loads the policy and serves it over gRPC.

```bash
python -m lerobot.async_inference.policy_server \
  --host=0.0.0.0 \
  --port=8080 \
  --fps=30
```

--------------------------------

### Inference Backends > Real-Time Chunking (`--inference.type=rtc`)

Source: https://github.com/huggingface/lerobot/blob/main/docs/source/inference.mdx

A background thread produces action chunks asynchronously. The main control loop polls for the next ready action while the policy computes the next chunk in parallel.

Use RTC with large, slow VLA models (Pi0, Pi0.5, SmolVLA) for smooth, continuous motion despite high inference latency.

entities.name: RT-2 / Vision-Language-Action Models — Technical Summary + Current Tooling
observations: SOURCE: "RT-2: Vision-Language-Action Models Transfer Web Knowledge to Robotic Control", Brohan et al. (Google DeepMind), 2023, arXiv:2307.15818v1, 26 pages. Local file: pdf/embodied_ai_papers/RT-2, Vision-Language-Action Models Transfer Web Knowledge to Robotic Control, Anthony Brohan et al., 2023, v1_compressed.pdf. Knowledge item created 2026-11-01.

CORE IDEA: A VLA (vision-language-action) model is a pretrained vision-language model co-fine-tuned to emit robot actions directly. Actions are expressed as text tokens and trained with the same next-token objective as language, so image + instruction -> low-level action runs end-to-end in one model with fully shared weights (no separate action head or action-only layers).

ACTION ENCODING (paper Sec. 3.2): 8 integers per step = [terminate, dpos_x, dpos_y, dpos_z, drot_x, drot_y, drot_z, gripper_extension]. 6-DoF end-effector delta pose + gripper + episode-termination flag; all continuous dims discretized into 256 uniform bins. Emitted as a whitespace-separated string, e.g. "1 128 91 241 5 101 127".

TOKEN MAPPING: 256 tokens must be reserved as action vocabulary. PaLI-X already has a unique token per integer up to 1000, so bins map to those integer tokens; PaLM-E has no such representation, so its 256 least-frequently-used tokens are overwritten (a form of symbol tuning).

TRAINING FORMAT: robot camera image + instruction are posed in standard VQA form ("Q: what action should the robot take to [instruction]? A: <action tokens>"), so manipulation data becomes another vision-language task.
BACKBONES: RT-2-PaLI-X built on PaLI-X (5B and 55B); RT-2-PaLM-E built on PaLM-E 12B. Both are {image, text} -> {text} VLMs.

CO-FINE-TUNING IS THE KEY TRICK: fine-tune on robot trajectories *mixed with* the original web-scale VLM data (VQA, captioning, interleaved image-text) instead of robot data alone. This prevents catastrophic forgetting of web concepts and measurably improves generalization; the robot dataset is up-weighted in each batch to keep the mixture balanced.

OUTPUT CONSTRAINT: at decode time the vocabulary is restricted to valid action tokens when the prompt is a robot-action task, while language/VQA prompts still allow the full natural-language vocabulary. Guarantees executable actions.

REAL-TIME INFERENCE: the 55B model is served on a multi-TPU cloud service queried over the network (simultaneously serving multiple robots), giving 1-3 Hz for 55B and ~5 Hz for 5B. Compute cost/latency is the main deployment constraint.

DATA & EVAL SCALE: ~6,000 real-robot evaluation trajectories; training data is the RT-1 dataset (13 robots, 17 months, office kitchen) plus web VLM data; 7-DoF mobile manipulator; 200+ seen tasks and 280+ unseen tasks.

RESULTS: seen-task performance roughly matches RT-1, but generalization to unseen objects/backgrounds/environments is ~2x better than RT-1 and MOO and ~6x better than other baselines. Emergent symbol understanding ("move apple to 3"), reasoning (same-color matching, arithmetic, multilingual commands) and human recognition average >3x RT-1's success rate.

ABLATIONS: 55B > 5B for generalization; training a large model from scratch performs poorly even at 5B; co-fine-tuning beats robot-only fine-tuning at every size. Simulated Language-Table: RT-2-PaLI-3B 90+-10 vs LAVA 77, RT-1 74, BC-Zero 72.

CHAIN-OF-THOUGHT: a few hundred gradient steps of data augmented with a natural-language "Plan:" step before the action tokens ("Instruction: I'm hungry. Plan: pick rxbar chocolate. Action: ...") bridges VQA-style reasoning and manipulation, enabling multi-stage semantic inference (pick a rock as an improvised hammer; choose an energy drink for a tired person).

LIMITATIONS: web pretraining transfers semantic/visual concepts but no new *physical* skills — the motion repertoire stays bounded by the robot dataset; inference compute/latency limits high-frequency control (quantization/distillation flagged as future work); few VLMs expose fine-tuning APIs.

MODERN EQUIVALENTS (verified in Context7 docs, 2026-11): Hugging Face LeRobot (/huggingface/lerobot, v0.6.1) is the closest current best-practice stack — `lerobot-train --policy.type=smolvla --policy.load_vlm_weights=true --dataset.repo_id=...` or `--policy.type=pi0 --policy.pretrained_path=lerobot/pi0_base`, plus dataset/env flags and standard steps/batch_size hyperparameters.

MODERN SERVING PATTERN: LeRobot async inference (install `.[async]`) splits a GPU policy server (`python -m lerobot.async_inference.policy_server --host --port`) from a robot client (`python -m lerobot.async_inference.robot_client --server_address --policy_type=smolvla|pi0 --actions_per_chunk=50 --chunk_size_threshold=0.5 --aggregate_fn_name=weighted_average`) — the direct descendant of RT-2's cloud-served 55B model. `--inference.type=rtc` (real-time chunking) is recommended for large slow VLAs (Pi0, Pi0.5, SmolVLA) to keep motion smooth despite latency.

MODERN BACKBONE PATH: Transformers (/websites/huggingface_co_transformers_v4_56_2_en) PaliGemma / PaliGemma2 via `image-text-to-text` pipeline or `PaliGemmaForConditionalGeneration` + `PaliGemmaProcessor`; note PaliGemma is not conversational and is meant to be fine-tuned per task (VQA, captioning, detection), and the processor's `suffix=` argument generates fine-tuning labels — the natural place to put action-token targets.

PRACTICAL MAPPING OF RT-2 RECIPE TODAY: (1) collect demonstrations in LeRobot dataset format with language instructions; (2) start from a VLM-backed policy (SmolVLA, pi0/pi0.5) and keep VLM weights loaded; (3) co-train on task data plus general VLM/VQA data to preserve semantics; (4) constrain decoding to the action vocabulary and discretize/bucket continuous action dims; (5) serve the policy on a GPU host via the async server and stream action chunks to the robot.
VERIFICATION CAVEAT: OpenVLA could not be confirmed — the Context7 resolver returned unrelated libraries (OpenClaw/OpenLayers/OpenBLAS) for that name, so no OpenVLA documentation was verified here.

entities.name: LeRobot
observations: Hugging Face LeRobot — end-to-end learning for robotics; Context7 ID /huggingface/lerobot, v0.6.1, High source reputation, ~4543 code snippets.

Provides `lerobot-train` CLI with policy types including smolvla, pi0, pi05, act; supports loading pretrained VLM weights, gradient checkpointing, bfloat16, frozen/unfrozen vision encoders, and train-expert-only modes.

Provides async inference (policy_server + robot_client over gRPC) and real-time chunking (RTC) for high-latency VLA policies; key tuning knobs are actions_per_chunk, chunk_size_threshold, aggregate_fn_name.
Documented datasets include lerobot/libero, lerobot/libero_plus, lerobot/metaworld_mt50 with matching env types for sim evaluation.

entities.name: Hugging Face Transformers (PaliGemma / VLM models)
observations: Context7 ID /websites/huggingface_co_transformers_v4_56_2_en — model-definition framework for text, vision, audio and multimodal models, ~11081 code snippets, High reputation.
PaliGemma/PaliGemma2 are supported as image-text-to-text models via `pipeline(task="image-text-to-text")` or `PaliGemmaForConditionalGeneration` + `AutoProcessor`.
PaliGemma is not designed as a conversational model; it performs best when fine-tuned for a specific task such as VQA, captioning, detection, or document understanding.
PaliGemmaProcessor handles images, text, and optional labels; passing `suffix=` produces the labels used during fine-tuning — the mechanism to adapt to text-encoded action targets.
